notes.summary: Idioms and phrases are fixed expressions whose meaning cannot be worked out from the individual words, such as 'to bury the hatchet' (to make peace). SSC CGL asks for the meaning of an idiom on its own or inside a sentence, and sometimes asks which idiom best fills a blank; the wrong options usually describe the literal picture of the words.
keyPoints: Never translate word for word: 'to smell a rat' has nothing to do with rats; it means to suspect that something is wrong. An option that describes the literal picture is almost always a distractor.
Use the sentence: in context questions, the tone (praise, criticism, failure, success) tells you whether the idiom's meaning is positive or negative.

Body-part idioms: take to one's heels (run away), feet of clay (a hidden weakness in an admired person), pay through the nose (pay far too much), turn a deaf ear (refuse to listen), keep one's fingers crossed (hope for success).

Colour idioms: red-letter day (a memorable, happy day), white elephant (a costly but useless possession), in black and white (in writing), green with envy (very jealous), out of the blue (unexpectedly), red tape (excessive official formality).

Conflict and peace: bury the hatchet (make peace), cross swords (quarrel), at daggers drawn (bitterly hostile), at loggerheads (in strong disagreement), at sixes and sevens (in confusion and disorder).

Decision and effort: burn one's boats or bridges (take a step with no way back), by hook or by crook (by any means), leave no stone unturned (try every possible way), at the eleventh hour (at the last moment).
Argument and reasoning: hold water (be logically sound), throw cold water on (discourage), a wild goose chase (a hopeless search), a cock-and-bull story (an unbelievable, made-up story).
Learn look-alike idioms in pairs: cry wolf (raise a false alarm) vs cry over spilt milk (regret what cannot be undone); in hot water (in trouble) vs throw cold water on (discourage).
traps: Choosing the literal meaning, such as 'hide weapons' for bury the hatchet or 'travel by sea' for burn one's boats.
Picking an option that could be true of the situation in the sentence but is not what the idiom means.
Reading a positive idiom as negative because of one word, such as taking 'red-letter day' to mean a day of danger.
In fill-in-the-blank idiom questions, choosing an idiom that is correct English but does not fit the logic of the sentence.
notes.examTip: If you have never seen the idiom, strike out every option that merely describes the literal words, then use the tone of the sentence to choose between the options that remain.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A red-letter day
questions.explanation:
The idiom comes from the old practice of marking important festival days in red ink on calendars.
It therefore refers to a special day that is remembered with happiness, such as the day one gets a first job.
Red does not signal danger here, so the first option is a trap.
The meaning is a memorable and happy day.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To smell a rat
options: To suspect that something is wrong
To live in a dirty place
questions.explanation:
The idiom is not about rats or smells; it means to sense that something is not right.
Example: When the stranger offered a prize for a small fee, she smelt a rat.
The other options are based on the literal words.
The meaning is to suspect that something is wrong.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To take to one's heels
questions.explanation:
Showing your heels to someone means you are moving away from them quickly.
Example: The thief took to his heels when he saw the police.
Kicking and following are literal readings of 'heels'.
The meaning is to run away.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
At sixes and sevens
options: In a state of confusion and disorder
questions.explanation:
The idiom describes things or people that are disorganised or confused.
Example: After the sudden transfer of the manager, the whole office was at sixes and sevens.
The options about gambling and calculations come from the numbers in the idiom, and 'perfect order' is the opposite.
The meaning is in a state of confusion and disorder.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
A white elephant
options: A costly possession that is more trouble than it is worth
questions.explanation:
A white elephant is something that costs a lot to own or maintain but gives little benefit.
Example: The huge stadium built for a single event became a white elephant for the city.
The options about an animal, strength or luck are literal or symbolic readings.
The meaning is a costly possession that is more trouble than it is worth.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom used in the sentence.
After years of bitter quarrels over the boundary wall, the two neighbours finally decided to bury the hatchet.
options: To prepare for a final fight
To make peace and end the quarrel
questions.explanation:
A hatchet is a small axe, and burying it symbolised giving up fighting.
The sentence contrasts 'years of bitter quarrels' with 'finally decided', which signals an end to the conflict.
'Hide their weapons' is the literal reading, and dividing the land is not the meaning of the idiom.
The meaning is to make peace and end the quarrel.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom used in the sentence.
The defence lawyer's argument did not hold water, so the judge rejected it.
questions.explanation:
An argument that 'holds water' is sound, like a container without leaks.
So 'did not hold water' means the argument had flaws and could not stand up to examination.
The judge rejecting it confirms the negative meaning.
The meaning is was not logical or convincing.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom used in the sentence.
Her father threw cold water on her plan to open a bakery.
questions.explanation:
To throw cold water on something is to be unenthusiastic about it and discourage it.
Supporting the plan enthusiastically is the opposite meaning.
Examining or postponing the plan does not carry the sense of dampening someone's hopes.
The meaning is discouraged the plan.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.
The determined manager has promised to finish the project before the deadline _____.
questions.explanation:
The words 'determined' and 'promised' show that the manager will finish the work whatever it takes.
'By hook or by crook' means by any means possible.
'In a nutshell' means in brief, 'at sixes and sevens' means in confusion, and 'in cold blood' means deliberately and cruelly; none fits the logic.
The answer is by hook or by crook.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To have feet of clay
options: To be very slow in work
To have a hidden weakness despite being admired
To be firmly rooted in one's beliefs
questions.explanation:
The idiom comes from the story of a statue with a head of gold but feet partly made of clay, which could easily be broken.
It describes a respected or admired person who turns out to have a serious flaw.
It has nothing to do with slowness, humility or firm beliefs.
The meaning is to have a hidden weakness despite being admired.

questions.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
To burn one's boats
options: To take a step that leaves no way back
questions.explanation:
Soldiers who burnt their boats after landing could not retreat, so they had to go forward.
The idiom means to commit to a course of action so fully that one cannot return to the earlier position.
Example: By resigning from his government job to start a business, he burnt his boats.
The meaning is to take a step that leaves no way back.
